quote: Gilbert, Tafarodi, and Malone’s paper was entitled “You Can’t Not Believe Everything You Read.”
content: The special case in which Spinoza's model fits, novel statements the reader cannot check, is the case the essay describes ("novel statements labeled true or false") and the one its advice concerns: the tabloid at the checkout. Nobody reads a supermarket newspaper to have their existing knowledge contradicted. The fast-rejection results also have limits in the other direction. Repetition makes statements more believable even when they contradict what subjects demonstrably know (Fazio et al. 2015), so knowledge does not simply shield the reader. The essay's title is a question, and it never claims Descartes was refuted. It reports a laboratory asymmetry and applies it where it holds.

quote: These non-busy participants recommended 7.03 years versus 6.03 years for criminals whose reports falsely exacerbated or falsely excused.
content: The essay did make it the headline of its advice: "we should be more careful when we expose ourselves to unreliable information, especially if we're doing something else at the time." It reports the non-busy figures in full, 7.03 against 6.03, so the reader can see the effect depends on load. Reading while doing something else is the ordinary condition of news consumption, not a laboratory curiosity. The continued-influence literature Fable brings in fits the essay's conclusion. Corrected misinformation keeps shaping inference even without distraction (Lewandowsky et al. 2012), so the "unbelieving" step is fragile in more ways than Gilbert tested. Fable finds that the conclusion is defensible, and a second literature arriving at the same place supports it.
